Tenancy, Identity & Access ​

Saidi runs one codebase for a laptop install and a hosted workspace. The seam that makes that possible is a tenant context: a small record saying who is acting inside which organization, carried implicitly through every call. Store lookups, filesystem paths, budgets, and permission checks all read that one record.

This page is the architecture behind the reference tables in Orgs, Auth & Permissions — read that page for the operator-facing summary.

The tenant context ​

TenantContext is the whole principal. It lives in an AsyncLocalStorage scope, so it follows await boundaries without being threaded through every signature.

FieldMeaning
orgIdThe acting workspace. Every store read and every path is scoped by it
userIdThe acting member. 'local' or 'system' for non-human scopes
roleowner | admin | member — the org role
platformRoleuser | superadmin — the platform (host) role, separate from org role
userName / userEmailDisplay identity, set only where the User record is already loaded
viaHow the scope entered: ui, ws, cron, reflex, telegram, run, system

Two accessors read it:

ts
tenant()        // throws in cloud mode if no scope was opened
tenantOrNull()  // never throws; null when no scope is open

The asymmetry is deliberate. A missing scope is a bug in an entry point, not a condition to paper over — so tenant() throws loudly rather than silently defaulting to some other org's data.

Per-org stores and paths ​

Each org gets its own set of the existing store classes — runs, crons, chats, reflexes, credits, playbooks — constructed with org-scoped persistence. The module singletons other code imports (runs, chats, …) are ambient() proxies: every property access resolves the current tenant's instance and forwards to it, so runs.list() at a call site is unchanged while returning a different set per org.

Each workspace's state nests one level under the platform data root:

orgs/<orgId>/
├── memory/   runs (incl. work/ and assets/), project + agent memory, global.md
├── agents/   AGENT.md dirs, skills, mcp.json
├── config/   org-visible config
└── repos/    server-side project clones

safeOrgId() rejects anything that isn't [A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,63} before an id is ever joined into a path, so a crafted org id cannot escape its own workspace root.

Structured records are filtered rather than pathed: the run persistence layer holds an optional orgId and folds { orgId } into every query. ensureOrgStores() hydrates an org's stores from Mongo exactly once and is awaited by every entry point before serving, so the synchronous store reads that follow see durable data.

Genuinely global files stay global: settings.json, secrets.json, and the legacy telegram.json deliberately use the module-level constants, not the org-scoped helpers.

Who opens a scope ​

Entry pointScope sourcevia
HTTP requestorgContext middleware — X-Saidi-Org header → membershipui
WebSocketUpgrade handler — cookie session + ?org= query paramws
Run turn / delegationtenantForRun(run) — the run's orgId + createdByrun
Cron firetenantForCron(job) — the job's orgId + createdBycron
Reflex firetenantForReflex(reflex)reflex
Boot / schedulerssystemTenant(orgId) — userId: 'system'system

Automations act as their creator, never as an anonymous org actor. A cron's fired run resolves the creator's budget, effort ceiling, and agent access; a run's every turn resolves against createdBy regardless of who enqueued the work. See Runs for how that interacts with sharing.

Authenticating a request ​

Cloud mode mounts four middlewares in order:

  1. csrfOriginCheck — for POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE, rejects a request whose Sec-Fetch-Site is cross-site, or whose Origin host matches neither the inbound Host nor the operator-declared SAIDI_PUBLIC_URL host (needed because a proxy rewrites Host). Defense in depth on top of the cookie's SameSite=Lax.
  2. requireSession — reads the saidi_session cookie, validates it, and stashes { user, session }; 401 otherwise.
  3. orgContext — reads X-Saidi-Org, verifies membership, loads the org and its stores, resolves the permission set, and opens the tenant scope that the rest of the handler chain runs inside.
  4. requirePermission(key) / requireOwner / requireSuperadmin — per-route gates mounted after the context resolver.

orgContext has two branches worth knowing: a suspended org still serves GET but returns 403 org_suspended on any mutation, and a platform superadmin who is not a member gets a virtual owner-level membership so they can open the workspace to inspect it — nothing is persisted for that spectate membership.

The WebSocket upgrade repeats the same checks at handshake time: an Origin allowlist (verifyClient), the session cookie, the ?org= membership check, and the same superadmin carve-out. It also tags the socket with runs.viewAll / chats.viewAll so broadcast frames can be scoped per socket rather than filtered per client.

Sessions and tokens as implemented ​

Every token in the auth stack is an opaque 32-byte random string rendered base64url. Only sha256(token) is stored — a database leak cannot yield a live session, password-reset link, or invite link.

TokenLifetimeNotes
Session30 days sliding, 90 days absoluteRenewed at most once an hour, to avoid a write per request
verify_email24 hoursOne-shot; consumed by an atomic findOneAndUpdate
reset_password1 hourSame one-shot consumption
Invite7 daysBound to an email address; re-issuing invalidates the old link
OAuth state10 minutesIn-process, single-use

The session cookie is saidi_session, set HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Path=/, with Secure added when the request arrived over HTTPS (directly or via a proxy setting X-Forwarded-Proto). Validation deletes an expired session, refuses a disabled user, and slides the expiry — capped at the absolute deadline. revokeAllSessions(userId) exists for password reset, disable, and removal.

Passwords use scrypt (N=16384, r=8, p=1, 32-byte key) with a minimum length of 10, stored self-describing as scrypt$N$r$p$salt$hash so cost parameters can be raised — or the algorithm swapped — without invalidating existing hashes.

Google and GitHub OAuth are an authorization-code redirect flow configured entirely by platform environment variables (SAIDI_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID/_SECRET, SAIDI_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID/_SECRET, with SAIDI_PUBLIC_URL as the redirect base) — see Settings. The login screen offers only the providers whose id and secret are set. The state is bound to the initiating browser by a short-lived saidi_oauth_state cookie carrying sha256(state), so a state minted in an attacker's browser cannot be replayed into a victim's. GitHub's profile email is often private, so the flow reads /user/emails to get a verified address before auto-linking.

The first account whose email matches SAIDI_SUPERADMIN_EMAIL becomes the platform superadmin, idempotently, on signup or login.

Secrets at rest ​

Tenant secrets — org webhook secrets, channel bot tokens, user connection tokens — use envelope encryption: AES-256-GCM under a random per-record data key, itself wrapped by a deployment master key from SAIDI_MASTER_KEY. Rotating the master key re-wraps the (tiny) data keys instead of re-encrypting payloads, and per-record keys bound the blast radius of any one disclosure.

SAIDI_MASTER_KEY accepts 64 hex characters or base64 for exactly 32 bytes; any other non-empty value is treated as a passphrase and stretched with scrypt so a low-entropy operator passphrase is not offline-brute-forceable against a captured blob. The platform refuses to boot without it, so a stored secret is never at rest in plaintext.

Roles and permissions in code ​

The permission catalog is a versioned constant, not a database table — adding a key is a code change with no migration. A membership stores only sparse overrides, which resolvePermissions(role, overrides) merges over the role defaults.

KeyOwnerAdminMember
runs.create, runs.approve✔✔✔
runs.viewAll, runs.steerAll, runs.approveAll✔✔—
chats.viewAll✔✔—
agents.manage, crons.manage, reflexes.manage, memory.manage✔✔—
usage.viewOrg, billing.view, members.manage✔✔—
settings.manage✔——
market.install.skill / .mcp / .agent / .department, market.publish✔✔—

There are deliberately no custom roles and no permission groups; both can layer on later without a schema change. Client-supplied overrides pass through sanitizeOverrides(), which keeps only known keys with boolean values.

Agent access is separate from permissions: AgentAccess is { mode: 'all' | 'allowlist' | 'denylist', agents }, and canUseAgent(access, name) is the gate PRIME's delegation consults before routing work to an agent.

Where the checks actually run ​

Permission checks happen at three layers, and they answer different questions:

  • Route gates — requirePermission(key) returns 403 permission_denied:<key> before a handler runs. Coarse, per-endpoint.
  • Per-object ACLs — canViewRun / canSteerRun combine ownership (createdBy), the sharedWith list, and the spectator flag. Every route that reads or mutates a run's data, git views, files, or assets goes through them.
  • Delivery scoping — scopeStateForUser() narrows the org-wide state snapshot at the point of delivery: runs filtered to own-plus-shared, chats likewise, agents and departments filtered to the member's allowlist, and the recent-activity feed restricted to chats the viewer can see so another member's transcript never rides along in the payload.

Budget enforcement sits in front of dispatch and reads the same ambient context, with memberships and orgs cached for ~30 seconds because it runs on every delegation. Per-member ceilings (MemberLimits) cover monthly credit budget, a one-time extra grant, a per-run cost cap that pauses rather than cancels, an effort ceiling that clamps rather than rejects, and a concurrent-run limit. 0 or '' means "no member-level limit".

The channel caveat ​

Chat channels are the one surface not yet wired into this model. startChannels() is called only when !isCloud(), and the Telegram inbound path authorizes against a flat global allow-list of Telegram user ids rather than resolving a per-member channel identity. The channel-identity registry exists but is not yet called by any adapter or route. Treat channel access as "this install's owner", not as per-member auth — see Connecting Telegram for what that means in practice.
